newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: US approves escrow account for "oil for food" deal.
newsitem.headline: US approves escrow account for "oil for food" deal.

text.p: The United States treasury has approved the opening of an escrow account in the New York branch of the Banque Nationale de Paris to hold the proceeds of an "oil-for-food" deal with Iraq, a U.N. source said Tuesday.
U.S. government approval was necessary because of sanctions imposed on Iraq after its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The source said the approval came through last Friday.

Under the oil-for-food deal signed by Iraq and the United Nations May 20, Iraq would be able to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months, on a renewable basis, to buy food, medicine and other humanitarian goods to help offset the effects of sanctions on ordinary Iraqis.

But it has not yet been implement because various arrangements had to be made, such as ensuring the food would be distributed equitably throughout Iraq and appointing U.N. monitors to check oil contracts in New York and to oversee the plan on the ground.

Arrangements had been near completion when Iraq sent its troops into the Kurdish-inhabited northern provinces at the end of August, prompting Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali to say the security situation prevented the deployment of the necessary U.N. staff.

Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller said in Istanbul Tuesday on her return from the U.N. General Assembly in New York that Boutros-Ghali had told her Iraq's oil pipeline to Turkey, which will carry much of the exported oil, would be reopened in a few weeks.
But U.N. spokesmen were unable Tuesday to give a firm date for when Boutros-Ghali might give the go-ahead for actual implementation of the oil-for-food arrangement.

On Monday, Under-Secretary-General Yasushi Akashi, who heads U.N. humanitarian operations, said in Geneva he hoped the plan would go into effect "in the near future," adding later that it might be "a matter of weeks."

Also on Monday, United States undersecretary of state for Near East affairs, Robert Pelletreau, said in New York that the deal could be implemented "in a matter of weeks...if the Kurdish factions can come to an agreement" so that the security situation there would not be a threat to U.N. monitors.

There has been speculation this might not occur before the November 5 elections in the United States, since permitting Iraq to export limited quantities of oil as a humanitarian exception to sanctions has become an issue between President Clinton and his Republican opponent, former Senator Bob Dole.
